title: How Will AI Affect the US Labor Market?
author: Goldman Sachs

dom.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Goldman Sachs supports the cluster’s cautious labour-market conclusion: realised displacement is currently concentrated in relatively small sectors, while broader effects remain forecasts contingent on adoption speed. Its projected worker displacement is more substantial than current legal-employment evidence, but the modest aggregate unemployment estimate and expected job creation remain consistent with heterogeneous pressure rather than demonstrated profession-wide replacement.
qs: Apart from tech workers, others in the knowledge and creative sectors, such as management consultants, call center workers, and graphic designers, have also seen some displacement of their labor by AI, but these are relatively small parts of the overall job market.
In Briggs' base case, the timeline for firms to adopt AI on a wide scale is around 10 years, and 6-7% of workers will be displaced during that transition period.

kp.k: AI displacement remains concentrated in particular employment niches
kp.d: Joseph Briggs, co-leader of Goldman Sachs Research's global economics team, attributes below-trend tech employment share and some displacement among management consultants, call center workers, and graphic designers to AI. The article qualifies these observations: affected sectors are relatively small, and labor data have not yet shown significant AI-led changes in the overall US employment mix.
qs: "You can see AI's impact in the tech sector, where the employment share as a proportion of the whole economy has gone below the long term trend," he says.

Apart from tech workers, others in the knowledge and creative sectors, such as management consultants, call center workers, and graphic designers, have also seen some displacement of their labor by AI, but these are relatively small parts of the overall job market.
As yet, no significant AI-led changes in the employment mix across the whole US economy have shown up in labor data.

kp.k: Adoption speed determines projected unemployment disruption
kp.d: Briggs' base case anticipates widespread firm adoption over around 10 years, with 6-7% of workers displaced during the transition. Goldman Sachs Research projects a 0.6 percentage point unemployment-rate increase if the transition unfolds over a decade; Briggs warns that more frontloaded adoption would have substantially larger economic effects. These are conditional forecasts, not observed displacement totals.
qs: In Briggs' base case, the timeline for firms to adopt AI on a wide scale is around 10 years, and 6-7% of workers will be displaced during that transition period.
If it takes place over a decade, Goldman Sachs Research expects to see a 0.6 percentage point increase in the unemployment rate.
"But if it's more frontloaded, the impacts on the economy are much larger," Briggs says.

kp.k: Automation exposure extends beyond current observed displacement
kp.d: Goldman Sachs Research estimates that around 300 million jobs globally are exposed to AI automation. Briggs' team estimates that AI could automate tasks accounting for 25% of US work hours. These estimates concern potential exposure and task automation, distinct from the forecast share of workers displaced.
qs: Globally, around 300 million jobs are exposed to AI automation.
In the US, AI can potentially automate tasks that account for 25% of all work hours, Briggs' team finds.

kp.k: Displaced knowledge workers may face occupational mismatch
kp.d: GS SUSTAIN analyst Evan Tylenda suggests that workers displaced from knowledge industries may be poorly suited to the occupations most in demand. He identifies both low-skill, low-wage roles, including fast-food work, cleaning, and home healthcare, and skilled technical roles, including construction, engineering, electrical work, and linework.
qs: Workers who are likely to be displaced from the knowledge industries by AI may be less suited to the kinds of labor that are most needed, says Evan Tylenda, an analyst with GS SUSTAIN.
On the one hand, these include low-skill, low-wage jobs: fast-food workers, cleaners, home healthcare workers, for instance.
On the other hand, the market will also require more skilled technical work, of the kind provided by construction workers, engineers, electricians, and lineworkers.

kp.k: Power and data-center expansion generate demand for workers
kp.d: Tylenda forecasts that roughly 500,000 net new US jobs will need filling by 2030 to meet growing power demand. Briggs reports above-trend hiring for HVAC contractors, electrical contractors, and other data-center construction workers. The article reports an increase of 216,000 construction jobs exposed to the data-center build-out since 2022, while Briggs expects further data-center investment growth.
qs: In the US alone, Tylenda says, roughly 500,000 net new jobs will need to be filled to satisfy the growing demand for power by 2030.
Relative to trend, the hiring for HVAC contractors, electrical contractors, and other workers to build data centers has risen.
Construction jobs exposed to the data center build-out have increased by 216,000 since 2022.
"And we expect that data center investment will continue to grow," he says.

kp.k: AI could create skilled and specialized occupations
kp.d: Beyond infrastructure employment, Briggs predicts greater demand for AI knowledge and associated skills, alongside new specialized occupations. Healthcare provides his historical analogy: previous technological advances enabled specialization. The article presents these as prospective job-creation mechanisms rather than quantified employment findings.
qs: Beyond the infrastructure sector, Briggs says, the AI revolution can create three new kinds of jobs.
There will be an increase in demand for workers with AI knowledge and associated skills.
AI will also create new, specialized occupations—in, for example, fields like healthcare, where technological advancements in the past have made specialization possible.

kp.k: Income gains could indirectly expand discretionary service employment
kp.d: Briggs' third proposed job-creation mechanism is indirect demand growth arising from higher incomes, demand, and worker availability, including roles that were already technologically feasible. As a historical illustration, the article states that 1 million workers currently work in pet care, nail salons, educational support/tutoring, and athletic coaching occupations that emerged over the last 30 years; it does not attribute those existing jobs to AI.
qs: And finally, AI can indirectly boost discretionary demand in occupations that emerge because of rising incomes, demand, and worker availability, even if these roles were already technologically feasible.
For example, 1 million workers today are employed in pet care, nail salons, educational support/tutoring, and athletic coaching occupations that emerged over the last 30 years.

kp.k: Recent hiring slowdown is attributed to non-AI shocks
kp.d: Briggs dates slowing job growth to the second half of 2025. The article identifies tariff-related uncertainty, which reduced employers' hiring confidence, and sharply slowing immigration from its fast 2023 and 2024 pace as the two shocks behind that slowdown. Goldman Sachs Research expects net immigration to slow further in 2026.
qs: "ever since we started to see job growth slow in the second half of 2025."
The first was uncertainty related to tariffs, which made employers less confident about hiring.
The second was the dramatic slowing of immigration into the US, from a fast pace in 2023 and 2024.
Goldman Sachs Research expects net immigration to further slow this year.

kp.k: Accelerated AI losses could undermine the 2026 labor outlook
kp.d: Briggs projects labor-market stabilization supported partly by fiscal tailwinds and other factors forecast to accelerate GDP growth sharply in the first half of 2026. The article estimates unemployment rising to 4.5% in 2026 from 4.3% in January. Briggs identifies earlier-than-expected AI job losses as a conditional downside risk that could prompt Federal Reserve rate cuts.
qs: But Briggs also projects a stabilization of the labor market, driven in part by fiscal tailwinds and other factors that are forecast to lead to a sharp acceleration in GDP growth in the first half of 2026.
Unemployment is estimated to inch up to 4.5% this year (from 4.3% in January).
"If we see some job losses pulled forward, that sets stage for potential underperformance relative to our forecast, and that may lead the Federal Reserve to cut rates."

kp.k: Entry-level knowledge workers face uncertain heightened exposure
kp.d: The article predicts that entry-level workers in their 20s and 30s entering knowledge and content creation sectors are likely to be most affected by new AI deployments. Briggs explicitly qualifies this prediction as uncertain and recommends monitoring labor-market data in real time.
qs: Entry-level workers in their 20s and 30s, coming into the knowledge and content creation sectors, are likely to be most affected by new deployments of AI.
"But this is not a foregone conclusion," Briggs says.
"There's a lot of uncertainty about how this will play out. It's important to watch the labor market data in real time to monitor that," he adds.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Goldman Sachs Research and Joseph Briggs predict substantial AI exposure and transitional worker displacement, while distinguishing these from economy-wide employment changes already observed.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about labor markets, not a source making legal-services-specific predictions. Goldman Sachs Research estimates that 300 million jobs globally are exposed to AI automation and that tasks accounting for 25% of US work hours could be automated; these are exposure and task-automation estimates, not counts of predicted job losses. Briggs' base case anticipates broad firm adoption over approximately 10 years, with 6–7% of workers displaced during the transition and a 0.6 percentage point increase in unemployment if the transition takes a decade. He says faster displacement would produce larger economic impacts. Briggs identifies existing effects in technology employment; the article also reports some displacement among management consultants, call center workers and graphic designers, but says significant AI-led shifts in the overall US employment mix have not yet appeared in labor data.

pts.k: Briggs and Evan Tylenda predict AI-related job creation, especially in infrastructure, but warn that displaced knowledge workers may not match the jobs in demand.
pts.d: Tylenda estimates that roughly 500,000 net new US jobs will need to be filled by 2030 to meet growing power demand. Briggs reports increased hiring associated with data-center construction and expects data-center investment to keep growing. Beyond infrastructure, he identifies three potential job-creation channels: demand for AI skills, new specialized occupations, and occupations supported indirectly by rising incomes, demand and worker availability. Tylenda cautions that displaced knowledge workers may be less suited to both low-wage service work and skilled technical jobs needed by the market. The article also broadly presents AI as promising productivity gains and help filling labor-market gaps.

pts.k: Briggs identifies accelerated AI job losses as a conditional downside risk to the 2026 labor-market outlook, particularly for entry-level knowledge and content workers.
pts.d: Briggs forecasts labor-market stabilization and unemployment of 4.5% in 2026, up from 4.3% in January, but says AI losses pulled forward could cause underperformance and potentially prompt Federal Reserve rate cuts. The article identifies entry-level workers in their 20s and 30s entering knowledge and content-creation sectors as likely to be most affected, while Briggs explicitly rejects treating this outcome as certain. The article attributes the preceding slowdown in job growth to tariff uncertainty and slower immigration, rather than presenting that broad slowdown as evidence of AI displacement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article relies on Goldman Sachs analyst estimates, reported labor-market trends and historical analogies; it does not provide underlying datasets or modeling methods.
pts.d: Automation exposure, displacement and unemployment effects are attributed to Goldman Sachs Research or Briggs' team, while the power-sector jobs projection is attributed to Tylenda. The stated observational basis includes technology employment's share falling below its long-term trend, above-trend hiring for data-center-related contractors, and 216,000 additional construction jobs exposed to data-center buildout since 2022. The reported displacement in consulting, call centers and graphic design is not quantified. Healthcare specialization and the approximately 1 million workers now in selected occupations that emerged over the past 30 years illustrate possible job-creation mechanisms; they are historical analogies, not evidence that AI has already created those jobs. No specific datasets, causal identification methods or forecast calculations are supplied in the article.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source separates current niche effects from a roughly decade-long adoption scenario, a 2030 infrastructure projection and conditional risks during 2026.
pts.d: Published March 18, 2026, the article describes sector-specific displacement as already occurring but qualifies that aggregate employment-mix changes are not yet evident. The adoption and displacement base case spans approximately 10 years; the 0.6 percentage point unemployment increase is conditional on a decade-long transition, with larger impacts if it is frontloaded. The article gives no separate explicit realization date for the global exposure or US automatable-hours estimates. Infrastructure evidence covers growth since 2022, and the power-demand employment projection runs to 2030. Broader new-occupation predictions have no precise deadline. For 2026, accelerated job losses and consequent rate cuts are possibilities rather than unconditional forecasts. Briggs stresses uncertainty and real-time monitoring.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Exposure is concentrated in knowledge and creative work, while anticipated opportunities extend to infrastructure workers, AI-skilled workers and new specialist or discretionary-service occupations.
pts.d: The article names technology workers, management consultants, call center workers and graphic designers as already experiencing effects or some displacement. Entry-level workers in their 20s and 30s entering knowledge and content-creation sectors are identified as especially vulnerable to new deployments. Displaced knowledge workers face potential skill mismatch with demand for fast-food workers, cleaners and home healthcare workers, as well as construction workers, engineers, electricians and lineworkers. HVAC and electrical contractors are identified as benefiting from data-center construction. Workers with AI knowledge and future specialists, including in healthcare, may gain opportunities. The exposure estimate is global, while the work-hours estimate and most employment discussion concern the US. No legal profession, law-firm segment or legal client group is singled out.
